hints: Follow air from the outside inward - trachea to bronchus to bronchiole to alveolus. Think about where a stiff support to hold the tube open is most needed and where it would get in the way of gas exchange.
Remember the difference in cartilage between the two largest tubes. One has neat C-shaped incomplete rings only, the other has more broken-up irregular plates as it branches.
Think about the smallest structures. Which one still needs a little smooth muscle to control airflow, and which one is just a thin wall for diffusion with no muscle at all?
walkthrough:
Why Large Airways Need Cartilage and Small Ones Do Not**
Think of cartilage as stiff support to stop airways collapsing when pressure changes during breathing. The trachea and bronchus are large and need this support. As tubes get smaller, cartilage disappears to allow flexibility and then disappears completely where diffusion must happen.

Sorting Trachea and Bronchus by Cartilage Shape**
The trachea is the single windpipe. It has regular C-shaped incomplete rings only. The gap in the C lets the oesophagus expand during swallowing. The bronchus branches off and has more irregular plates plus some incomplete rings because the wall structure becomes less regular.

Sorting Bronchiole and Alveolus by Muscle**
Both bronchioles and alveoli have no cartilage. Bronchioles still have smooth muscle present to constrict and control air flow to different lung regions. Alveoli are tiny air sacs for gas exchange, so they have neither cartilage nor smooth muscle - just very thin squamous epithelium.
Final answer: irregular plates and incomplete rings = bronchus; incomplete rings only = trachea; cartilage absent (smooth muscle present) = bronchiole; smooth muscle absent = alveolus.

hints: Start with what is actually in tobacco smoke that damages cells. Think about the sticky black component and the general name for chemicals that cause cancer.
Link that chemical damage to DNA and cell division. What happens to genes that control the cell cycle if their base sequence is changed?
walkthrough:
From Smoke Chemicals to Damaged DNA**
Tobacco smoke contains tar which includes many carcinogens. These are mutagens, meaning they interact with DNA in lung epithelial cells and change the base sequence. That is a gene mutation.

From Mutation to Cancer**
If mutation affects genes controlling cell division, control is lost. For example a proto-oncogene mutates to an active oncogene, or a tumour suppressor gene is switched off. The cell then divides by uncontrolled mitosis, forming a tumour - lung cancer.

Final answer: Tobacco smoke contains tar / carcinogens which are mutagenic and cause mutations e.g. proto-oncogene to oncogene or inactivation of tumour suppressor gene, leading to uncontrolled mitosis.

hints: Look carefully at tissue X in Fig. 5.2. Count how many cells thick it is from the lumen down to the smooth muscle, and compare that with the normal thin lining of an airway.
Recall what a healthy bronchus or bronchiole lining looks like - a single layer with two distinct cell types and hair-like structures on top. Check which of those features you can still see in X.
Zoom in on individual cells in X. Look at their shape, how similar they are to each other, and the size of their dark-stained nuclei compared with tall columnar cells.
walkthrough:
What Healthy Lining Should Look Like**
A healthy large airway is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. That means essentially one layer of tall columnar cells, some ciliated for moving mucus and some goblet cells for secreting mucus, with cilia facing the lumen.

What Tissue X Actually Shows**
Tissue X is much thicker, with many layers of cells piled up instead of one layer. All the cells look similar, with no obvious goblet cells. The surface has no cilia. The cells are flatter, smaller and more cubical than tall columnar cells, and their nuclei look large and prominent.

Making Paired Comparisons for Marks**
You only get marks for direct like-with-like comparisons. So state X versus healthy each time, for example: many layers present in X compared with few layers in healthy, no cilia in X compared with cilia present in healthy, cuboidal cells in X compared with columnar cells in healthy.

Final answer: Any three from: X has many layers / stratified v healthy has few / one layer; cells in X all same type v healthy has goblet cells and ciliated epithelial cells; cells in X flatter / smaller / cuboidal v healthy columnar; cilia absent in X; cells in X have large / prominent nuclei.
